recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: The transaction chain is broken: only 5,000 of 60,000 bills, diagnoses and payments link to an appointment, and facility/doctor/department disagree on ~95% of appointments.
recommendations.Recommendation: Fix the data pipeline first: enforce appointment-ID foreign keys, derive facility from the department/doctor hierarchy, and add the missing admissions, lab, prescription, referral and facility-master tables before any further modelling.
recommendations.Expected benefit: Critical enabler for every other analysis

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: The brief's headline questions on admissions, length of stay, bed use and referrals cannot be answered: no admission data exist and all 2,000 beds are 'Available'.
recommendations.Recommendation: Record bed status in real time (occupied/cleaning/out of service) and capture admission and discharge timestamps.

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: 75% of patients carry a chronic condition with no gradient by age, sex or province (tests 5-7, all non-significant after correction); 1,005 under-18s are recorded with hypertension. The rule-based flag marks 5,028 patients (25%) as high risk.
recommendations.Recommendation: Audit chronic-condition coding (especially for children). Until validated, use a universal chronic-care outreach for flagged high-risk patients (age 65+ with a chronic condition, or any chronic condition with a severe diagnosis) rather than age/sex/region targeting.
recommendations.Expected benefit: Reaches the 5,028 flagged patients; avoids mis-targeting

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: 40% of all 21,064 ratings are 1-2. No facility or department differs significantly (tests 2 and 4), and no clinical, financial or operational variable predicts rating (R² ≤ 0). Text comments contradict ratings in 30% of cases.
recommendations.Recommendation: Treat poor satisfaction as a network-wide service problem, not a site problem: run a network-wide patient-journey review (waiting, communication, billing). Link every survey to its appointment, and replace free-text comments with structured reason codes.
recommendations.Expected benefit: Targets the ~40% unhappy patients; makes future drivers measurable

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: Doctor workload ranges 5-28 appointments (P90/P10 = 1.9x); facility load per clinical staff member differs by 32% (HF013 highest, HF004 lowest), while rosters are almost identical (57-60 staff). Facility volume gaps are marginal (p=0.052).
recommendations.Recommendation: Pilot a scheduling rule that balances doctor panels, and move 2-3 clinical staff from the lowest-load sites (HF004, HF005, HF007) to the highest-load sites (HF013, HF014, HF011); re-measure after one quarter before a permanent change.
recommendations.Expected benefit: Narrows a ~32% load gap at no extra headcount

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: 0.92bn RWF (9.9% of billings) is unpaid across 11,887 underpaid bills, yet Billing.Status is unrelated to what was paid (test 9). 21,028 insurance claims (2.44bn RWF) are still pending, spread evenly over four insurers.
recommendations.Recommendation: Rebuild payment status from payment records (Amount - AmountPaid), start a collections list for the largest underpaid bills, and set a claim turnaround target for all four insurers (e.g. clear pending claims within 30 days).
recommendations.Expected benefit: Up to 0.92bn RWF of receivables and 2.44bn RWF of claims in play

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: The management revenue summary (1.13bn RWF) does not reconcile with billing (9.31bn RWF) and swings 66M-146M a month independent of volume (rho = 0.33, p = 0.30).
recommendations.Recommendation: Reconcile finance reporting to the billing ledger monthly and explain the May, September and November spikes before using revenue forecasts for budgeting.

recommendations.Evidence from the analysis: Demand is flat (no trend in monthly appointments, diagnoses or revenue; all p > 0.05) and no department, diagnosis or facility is growing. Cardiology (544) and Radiology (525) are the busiest department types but not significantly so.
recommendations.Recommendation: Do not commit capital to expansion on this evidence. Re-run the demand forecast once 24+ months of complete data exist, and use Cardiology and Radiology as the first capacity-review candidates.

figures.title: Patient profile of 20,000 registered patients
figures.interpretation: The register is almost perfectly balanced by sex (49.5% female) and spans all ages evenly (mean 45, no young-adult or elderly skew); the seven blood groups and 15 insurance plans are also near-uniform. Real populations are age-skewed and O+ is normally the most common blood group, while here only 7 of the 8 ABO/Rh groups appear (AB- is absent), which strongly suggests simulated data.

figures.title: Chronic disease burden by age group
figures.interpretation: Prevalence is flat at ~75% in every age band (range 73-76%), and children carry the same burden as the elderly (1,005 under-18s are recorded with hypertension and 984 with diabetes). Biologically, chronic disease should rise sharply with age, so age cannot be used as a risk signal in this dataset.

figures.title: Patients and chronic prevalence by province (schematic tile map)
figures.interpretation: Registered patients are spread evenly (3,923-4,091 per province) and chronic prevalence differs by under 2 points between provinces. A schematic tile map is used because district/sector/village names are placeholders and no boundary geometry exists, so a true geographic map is not possible.

figures.title: Patient growth proxy (no registration date exists)
figures.interpretation: First-time patients fall from 416 in January to 311 in December (slope -8.7 a month, p<0.001). This is a counting artifact, not shrinking demand: as the year goes on more patients have already been seen, so fewer appointments can be a 'first' visit, while total appointments stay flat (~417 a month). 4,443 of 20,000 registered patients (22.2%) appear in the extract; true patient growth needs a registration date.

figures.title: Clinical mix: diagnoses, severity and visit type
figures.interpretation: The five diagnoses each account for 18-21% of appointments (top: Hypertension, 21.2%); severity is split roughly one-third each, and 33.0% of visits are emergencies. A mix this even is unusual for real clinical data: for example malaria, hypertension and diabetes should not be equally common.

figures.title: Which diseases are becoming more common?
figures.interpretation: Every diagnosis fluctuates around ~83 cases a month with no significant upward or downward trend (smallest Holm-adjusted p = 0.49), so no disease can be called 'increasing' on this evidence; month-to-month moves are noise.

figures.title: Operational workload: doctors, facilities and departments
figures.interpretation: Doctor load is roughly Poisson-like (5-28 appointments, mean 14.3); facility volume ranges 217-278 (HF013 busiest, HF019 quietest) but differs from an even split only marginally (chi-square p=0.052, not significant after multiple-test correction); department volumes are consistent with an even split (p=0.49). Staffing is almost identical across facilities (57-60 clinical staff), so busy sites are not staffed any differently.

figures.title: Which departments are likely to be overloaded?
figures.interpretation: At individual-department level the workload index varies widely (36-195) mainly because rostered staff per department ranges 4-9 while appointment counts are near-uniform; at department-type level the spread is narrow (4.0-4.6 appointments per staff member), led by Cardiology. Overload risk is therefore a staffing-allocation issue more than a demand issue.

figures.title: Financial overview of 60,000 bills
figures.interpretation: Bills are uniformly spread between 10k and 300k RWF (mean 155k). 80.2% of bills are fully paid and the rest are underpaid by 0-50%, leaving 0.92bn RWF (9.9% of billings) outstanding, and the shortfall is the same whether a bill is labelled Paid, Partially Paid or Pending, so the status label carries no information. 50.0% of insurance claims are still pending.

figures.title: Monthly revenue: two sources that do not agree
figures.interpretation: Billed revenue from linked appointments is stable (~64M RWF a month, range 57-70M), whereas the management summary swings from 67M to 146M with peaks in May, September and November. Summary revenue is unrelated to summary appointment counts (Spearman rho=0.33, p=0.30), so the swings are not volume-driven and need finance to explain them.

figures.title: Patient satisfaction
figures.interpretation: Ratings are evenly spread across 1-5 (mean 2.99; 40.4% rate 1-2, 39.6% rate 4-5). Facility means (2.76-3.19) and department means (2.76-3.02) differ, but all confidence intervals overlap and the tests in section 6.3 show the gaps are within chance. 30.1% of responses have a text comment that contradicts the star rating.

figures.title: Correlation heatmap (Spearman, appointment level)
figures.interpretation: Apart from four structural pairs (visits count vs frequent-visitor flag; claim amount vs bill amount, as claims are 50-100% of the bill; severity vs the admission proxy that is built from it; prior visits vs month, which can only grow as the year progresses), no relationship is meaningful: the strongest remaining pair, PaidRatio vs Rating, has |rho| = 0.06. Age, chronic status, severity, billing and satisfaction are effectively independent in this dataset.

figures.title: Distributions and relationships: violin, box, scatter and density
figures.interpretation: Bills have the same distribution at every severity level and visit type, age has the same distribution for every chronic condition, and the age-billing regression line is flat (Spearman rho=-0.003, p=0.84). In real data, sicker and older patients would cost more; here cost is unrelated to either.

figures.title: Pair plot of key numeric variables (700-appointment sample)
figures.interpretation: No pair of variables shows a visible pattern or clustering by visit type; points fill each rectangle evenly. Discrete variables (severity score, prior visits) form horizontal and vertical bands only because they take few values.

figures.title: 12-month forecasts: patient volume and revenue (Tasks 1 and 2)
figures.interpretation: Models were chosen by back-test, and none of the series has a significant trend (p = 0.37 to 0.79), so forecasts are flat at the 2026 average. The wide bands, especially for the management revenue summary (CV 27%), mean month-level revenue cannot be predicted reliably from 12 data points.

figures.title: Department workload forecast, 2027 (Task 5)
figures.interpretation: The Mean model (chosen by back-test) forecasts ~42 appointments per department per month in the extract. The chance of exceeding the network's busiest-10% month (dotted line, 50) runs from 0% (ICU) to 24% (Cardiology), but department volumes do not differ significantly (chi-square p=0.49), so this ranking is a watch-list (Cardiology and Emergency first), not evidence of overload.

figures.title: Admission-proxy prediction (Task 3)
figures.interpretation: The best model (Gradient boosting) reaches AUC 0.501 (95% CI 0.477-0.527); an AUC of 0.50 is a coin flip, and its F1 (0.20) is no better than flagging every appointment (0.20). Every permutation importance is within noise of zero, so none of the available factors predicts the proxy and no admission-risk tool can be built from these variables.

figures.title: Patient satisfaction prediction (Task 4)
figures.interpretation: No model beats the mean-rating baseline (best R² = -0.000; negative means worse than guessing the average), and the best classifier's accuracy (38%) is no better than always predicting the majority class (41%). With importances at zero, satisfaction cannot be explained by diagnosis, severity, cost, payment, department, facility or doctor experience in this data.

figures.title: Patient segmentation (K-Means) and PCA
figures.interpretation: K-Means finds 4 segments (silhouette 0.22) but the shuffled-data null scores 0.18, so most of the apparent structure comes from a few discrete variables (visit count, claim filed or not, emergency or not) rather than natural groupings. PCA needs 6 of 7 components for 80% of the variance (first two: 29%), confirming the features are nearly uncorrelated and cannot be compressed meaningfully.

figures.title: Facility and department segmentation
figures.interpretation: Facilities split into a busier group of 9 sites (mean 264 appointments, 35% emergency visits) and a quieter group of 11 (mean 239, 31%); silhouette 0.21 vs shuffled null 0.17, stability ARI 0.92. The split is modest and volume gaps are only marginally significant, so treat it as a planning aid. Department clustering (k=6) scores 0.16 against a null of 0.17 with stability ARI 0.38, so it is no better than random grouping and should not be used.
